content: Scarlet fever is a disease mediated by exotoxins, most commonly associated with a sore throat and, less frequently, with impetigo or other streptococcal infections. It is characterized by symptoms such as a sore throat, fever, a strawberry tongue, and a fine, sandpaper-like rash that typically begins on the upper body and may spread to cover nearly the entire body. While scarlet fever is distinct from rheumatic fever, it can progress to this condition as the infection develops. Rheumatic fever is an autoimmune disease that can occur following an infection with Group A Streptococcus. Scarlet fever is an infectious disease that primarily affects children between the ages of 4 and 8. Its symptoms include a sore throat, fever, and a distinctive red rash. The disease is usually transmitted through inhalation of respiratory droplets. There is no vaccine available for scarlet fever, but it is effectively treated with antibiotics. Before the advent of antibiotics, scarlet fever was a significant cause of mortality and could lead to severe late complications such as glomerulonephritis and endocarditis, which often resulted in heart valve disease. These complications were prolonged and frequently fatal. The causative agent of scarlet fever is an erythrogenic toxin produced by the bacterium Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus) when it is infected by a specific bacteriophage. The term scarlatina is sometimes used interchangeably with scarlet fever, although it is more commonly employed to describe the milder form of the disease that has been observed since the early 20th century. Scarlet fever predominantly affects children, much like the common cold or flu. It is most frequently seen in individuals aged 3 to 15 years, with no significant difference in prevalence between males and females. By the age of 10, most children have developed protective antibodies, and the disease becomes rare in older individuals. The diagnosis of scarlet fever is primarily clinical. Laboratory findings may include marked leukocytosis with neutrophilia, elevated eosinophil counts, and increased levels of inflammatory markers such as ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) and CRP (C-reactive protein). Additionally, there is often an elevation in antistreptolysin O (ASO) titers. Blood cultures are rarely positive, but throat cultures can typically demonstrate the presence of streptococci. The treatment of scarlet fever is similar to that of streptococcal pharyngitis. Antibiotics are the mainstay of therapy, with penicillin being the first-line treatment. In cases of penicillin allergy, clindamycin or erythromycin can be used effectively. While antibiotic treatment is effective in managing the infection, it has not been conclusively shown to reduce the risk of developing rheumatic fever.
